title: Christian, recognize your dignity

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo meets Attila: the bishop of Rome walking north toward an army. Your line was he went out. Did you take one step toward that hard conversation? Day seven hundred forty-nine.

Same man, different day. Not on a road facing an invader this time, but in a church in Rome, on Christmas, preaching to a crowd. This sermon starts with joy: our Savior is born today, he tells them, so let us be glad, because there's no room for sadness on the birthday of Life. And then, partway through, he turns and speaks to each listener directly, as if pointing at them. Christian, recognize your dignity. The line has traveled a long way. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it today. Today's word is the one he called them by: Christian.
screen: `CHRISTMAS IN ROME.` → `NO ROOM FOR SADNESS.` → `HE SPEAKS TO EACH ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with what comes before the line. Leo has been preaching that in the birth of Jesus, God took on our human nature, so that people could share in God's own life. That's the whole engine of the sermon. Then comes the turn: Christian, recognize your dignity, and since you've been made a sharer in the divine nature, don't go back to your old meanness by the way you live. Next, the reminder. Leo tells them to remember whose body they belong to, and who its head is. Remember, he says, that you were rescued from the power of darkness and brought into God's light and kingdom. Notice what he's doing. He doesn't say: you are worthless, so try harder. He says the opposite. You have been given something enormous, so live like someone who has it. The dignity comes first. The living follows from it. The Catechism places this line at the opening of its section on the Christian life. Before it talks about any commandment, it reminds the reader who they are. Now the word itself. In the Acts of the Apostles, the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. For Leo's listeners, it was a name that tied them to Christ. When he calls out Christian, he isn't scolding a crowd. He's naming them. And a little look back at this week. Paula and Eustochium learning the book. Chrysostom honoring Christ in the poor. The Easter homily welcoming the eleventh hour. Patrick calling himself a sinner. Brigid with open hands. Leo going out. And today, Leo again, telling people their worth before telling them anything else.
screen: `GOD TOOK ON OUR NATURE.` · `RECOGNIZE YOUR DIGNITY.` · `WORTH FIRST, THEN LIVING.` · `A NAME TIED TO CHRIST.` · then, large: `KNOW YOUR DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat yourself with dignity today. Sit as if you were worth sitting well. Feet flat. Back long. Shoulders down. Breathe slowly. Now notice the voice in your head that talks to you through the day, the one that comments on your mistakes. Listen for its tone. Then try saying one thing to yourself the way you'd speak to someone you respect. Plainly, kindly, without flattery. If you pray, you can hear Leo's line as spoken to you: Christian, recognize your dignity. If you don't, simply rest in the posture of someone who matters. The bell holds the time.
Christian. A follower of Christ, the name the disciples were first called at Antioch, and the name Leo used to call his listeners to their dignity. Today's word.
Your line: know your dignity. Today, do one ordinary thing with care, as if you were worth the care: eat sitting down, dress with attention, or rest when you need to. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Leo's Christmas sermon in the Office of Readings at Christmas, and the Catechism opens its section on life in Christ with his line about recognizing one's dignity.

original.note: Latin: Christian, recognize your dignity — Leo's own words.

trapdoor: what you thought: dignity is something you earn by behaving well.
what it means: Leo says the dignity comes first, as a gift in Christ's birth, and good living follows from it.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism places this Christmas sermon at the very start of its teaching on life in Christ (CCC 1691).

notes: Leo, Sermon 21.1 (birth of our Savior, no place for sadness on the birthday of Life) and 21.3 (recognize your dignity, partner in the divine nature, do not return to former baseness, remember the head and body, rescued from the power of darkness into God's light and kingdom). All paraphrased; the Schaff/NPNF wording was not quoted because I couldn't confirm it word for word.
'Christian, recognize your dignity' is used as the index title and in voice as Leo's line, in the Catechism's English form; confirm acceptable without quotation marks.
CCC 1691 opens Part Three ('Life in Christ'). Confirm the 'section' wording.
howItsDone: the sermon is the Office of Readings for Christmas Day in the Liturgy of the Hours. Confirm.
